items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I was conducting the Lloyd Price band, and Tadd came to our performances.

ctx.x: Under what circumstances did you know him?

I got to know him. I was conducting the Lloyd Price band, and Tadd came to our performances. He and Miles came. We were playing at a club in the 80s. Miles would come in, and he wouldn’t go to the bar, and he wouldn’t go to a table. He’d go and sit in a corner, in a dark corner in the club and listen to the band. Then, when we’d come out, he’d say [Hampton imitates Davis’s voice], “The band sounds good,” and leave. That’s all he would – but he would come often to hear it. And Tadd came. Tadd came to me after one…
You had an association with Mingus.

items.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003
items.q: because I had worked with Lloyd Price’s band as the musical director

ctx.x: Well that was during the time when the trombone actually was becoming quite unpopular in the States. That was in the sixties after I had played with Dizzy’s band and Art Blakey and you weren’t hearing much about trombones doing any recordings or anything like that. But this guy Berry Gordy and some other people that knew about me because I had worked with Lloyd Price’s band as the musical director, so they wanted me to come out there. Because they actually wanted to start some kind of a jazz label. I don’t think…

meant. They didn’t mean the same thing that we might have meant. But when I went out there and I started working as a conductor, I was conducting shows, I was conducting Stevie Wonder and the Four Tops and all of that stuff, and some of the big shows and things. I went into some of the studios where they worked, I went to the studios and they had a way of writing that was really unique. I really — you couldn’t just be a good writer and go out there and take part in that. There was something special they had. And…
